newsitem.title: UK: Oil volatility exposes need for wider IPE data.
newsitem.headline: Oil volatility exposes need for wider IPE data.

text.p: With oil prices at five-year highs, traders and analysts are being robbed of a key weapon in their arsenal for predicting the next big price move in IPE Brent crude and gas oil futures -- a peek at what the big funds and commercial players are doing, and may do next.
A commitment of traders report released by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission gives clues into what those traders's positions are on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

But there is no counterpart for the IPE and industry sources said it would be of great interest and could even increase participation in the market because it shines a brighter light on what exactly is going on.
Such price transparency may also answer some questions as to how great a role the so-called speculators play in determining the price of oil.
"We've got blinders on" with regards the IPE market, said Philip Verleger, an energy economist at Charles River Associates in Washington, D.C.

"I've long been a critic of the U.S. markets but the reporting particularly through the CFTC and commitment of traders tends to make the U.S. market much more of a level playing field and tends to attract participants," he said.

For its part, the IPE recognizes the need for this information and said it would be willing to provide the data if it were required by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), the regulatory agency for the London futures markets.
"Based on what happened on the LME (London Metal Exchange) with Sumitomo it has really put that back on the agenda for the first time," an IPE spokesman said.
"It's under review and it's a possibility that those requirements may be implemented in the London markets," he said.
The IPE estimates that "...70 percent of incoming business is risk management related business from physical oil market participants," he said.

"It would help because the more information you have about the market the better it can function both among the players and those outside," said Leo Drollas, deputy director of the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London.

He also said there was a curious irony that some OPEC members believe the price of oil is set more by speculators than by the fundamentals of supply and demand, and therefore are discouraged from hedging in the futures market.
"It's not a gambler's paradise. It's a serious market which has evolved by the price volatility which was partly caused by OPEC," in the 1970s, he said.
"They were overconfident about their power and now they are less confident," he said, referring to OPEC. "It is a curious reversal of their perceptions."

The Centre said in a new study that hedgers help stabilize the market because they account for about two-thirds of the open interest in NYMEX crude oil and they adjust their price expectations more slowly, a counterbalance to the often "volatile price expectations" of the speculators.
"I'm not sure if it would actually increase volumes and open interest but I suppose it would provide more transparency," said Christopher Bellew, a director of Prudential Bache Futures in London.

"It may be a way of providing a comfort level for participants if they could see the commitments," he said, adding that high levels of open interest on Brent and gas oil have already attracted more business from funds.
The CFTC report details the long and short positions of those traders classified as commercial, non-commercial and non-reportable, as well as the net change on the week.
It also gives the number of traders in each category and the percent of total open interest that each category accounts for.
"I find it a useful statistic and we do quite a bit of analysis on the trader commitment report," said Peter Gignoux, manager of Smith Barney's petroleum desk in London.
But he noted that the CFTC data do not include activity in the over-the-counter market.
